chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Imitation as the principle common to the arts
paragraphs: My subject is Poetry in itself and its various kinds. I will note the essential quality of each kind, and ask how the plot must be structured if a poem is to be good. I will also ask how many parts a poem has and what they are, and take up whatever else belongs to the same inquiry. I follow the order of nature, and so begin with the first principles.

Epic poetry, Tragedy, Comedy and Dithyrambic poetry, and most music of the flute and of the lyre, are all, in their general conception, modes of imitation. They differ from one another in three ways: each has a different medium, different objects, and a different manner or mode of imitation.

Some people, by conscious art or by mere habit, imitate and represent various objects with color and form, or with the voice. In the same way, in the arts named above, taken as a whole, the imitation is produced by rhythm, language, or 'harmony,' used singly or in combination.

So the music of the flute and of the lyre uses 'harmony' and rhythm alone, and so do other arts that are essentially similar to these, such as playing the shepherd's pipe. Dancing uses rhythm alone, without 'harmony'; yet by rhythmical movement dancers too imitate character, emotion, and action.

There is another art that imitates by language alone, whether in prose or in verse. If it is in verse, it may mix different meters or keep to a single kind. This art has so far had no name. We have no common term for the mimes of Sophron and Xenarchus and the Socratic dialogues on the one hand, and for poetic imitations in iambic, elegiac, or any similar meter on the other. People do add the word 'maker' or 'poet' to the name of the meter, and speak of elegiac poets, or of epic (that is, hexameter) poets. They talk as if the imitation did not make the poet, and as if the verse alone entitled all of them, without distinction, to the name. Even when someone publishes a treatise on medicine or natural science in verse, custom gives its author the name of poet. Yet Homer and Empedocles have nothing in common except the meter, so it would be right to call the one a poet, and the other a physicist rather than a poet. By the same principle, suppose a writer in his poetic imitation were to combine all meters, as Chaeremon did in his Centaur, which is a medley of meters of every kind. We should still bring him under the general term poet. So much, then, for these distinctions.

Again, some arts use all the means mentioned above, namely rhythm, tune, and meter. Such are Dithyrambic and Nomic poetry, and also Tragedy and Comedy. The difference between them is this: the first two use all these means together, while the latter two use now one means, now another.
These, then, are the differences between the arts in the medium of imitation.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Objects of imitation
paragraphs: The objects of imitation are men in action. These men must be of a higher or a lower type, since moral character mainly follows these divisions, goodness and badness being what distinguish moral differences. It follows that we must represent men as better than in real life, or as worse, or as they are. Painting is the same. Polygnotus depicted men as nobler than they are, Pauson as less noble, and Dionysius drew them true to life.

Now it is evident that each of the modes of imitation mentioned above will show these differences. Each will become a distinct kind by imitating objects that are distinct in this way. Such differences may be found even in dancing, in flute-playing, and in lyre-playing. They are found in language too, whether prose or verse without music. Homer, for example, makes men better than they are, Cleophon makes them as they are, and Hegemon the Thasian, the inventor of parodies, and Nicochares, the author of the Deiliad, make them worse than they are. The same holds of Dithyrambs and Nomes: here too one may portray different types, as Timotheus and Philoxenus differed in representing their Cyclopes. The same distinction separates Tragedy from Comedy. Comedy aims at representing men as worse than in actual life, Tragedy as better.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Manner of imitation
paragraphs: There is still a third difference, the manner in which each of these objects may be imitated. The medium may be the same and the objects the same, and still the poet may imitate by narration. In that case he can either take on another personality, as Homer does, or speak in his own person without change. Or he may present all his characters as living and moving before us.

These, then, as we said at the beginning, are the three differences that distinguish artistic imitation: the medium, the objects, and the manner. So from one point of view Sophocles is an imitator of the same kind as Homer, for both imitate higher types of character. From another point of view he is of the same kind as Aristophanes, for both imitate persons acting and doing. Hence, some say, such poems are called 'drama,' because they represent action. For the same reason the Dorians claim to have invented both Tragedy and Comedy. The Megarians put forward the claim to Comedy. This is made not only by the Megarians of Greece proper, who say it arose under their democracy, but also by the Megarians of Sicily, since the poet Epicharmus, who is much earlier than Chionides and Magnes, came from that country. Certain Dorians of the Peloponnese claim Tragedy too. In each case they appeal to the evidence of language. They say that the outlying villages are called by them {kappa omega mu alpha iota}, and by the Athenians {delta eta mu iota}. They assume that Comedians got their name not from {kappa omega mu 'alpha zeta epsilon iota nu}, 'to revel,' but from wandering from village to village (kappa alpha tau alpha / kappa omega mu alpha sigma), because they were contemptuously shut out of the city. They add that the Dorian word for 'doing' is {delta rho alpha nu}, and the Athenian word is {pi rho alpha tau tau epsilon iota nu}.
This may be enough on the number and nature of the various modes of imitation.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Origin and development of poetry
paragraphs: Poetry in general seems to have sprung from two causes, both lying deep in our nature. First, the instinct of imitation is implanted in man from childhood. One difference between man and the other animals is that he is the most imitative of living creatures, and he learns his earliest lessons through imitation. No less universal is the pleasure people take in things imitated. Experience gives us evidence of this. We look with pain at some objects in themselves, yet we delight to contemplate them when they are reproduced with minute fidelity, such as the forms of the most ignoble animals and of dead bodies. The cause of this, again, is that learning gives the liveliest pleasure, not only to philosophers but to men in general, though their capacity for it is more limited. So men enjoy seeing a likeness because, in contemplating it, they find themselves learning or inferring, and saying perhaps, 'Ah, that is he.' For if you happen not to have seen the original, the pleasure will come not from the imitation as such, but from the execution, the coloring, or some other such cause.

Imitation, then, is one instinct of our nature. Next there is the instinct for 'harmony' and rhythm, meters being plainly sections of rhythm. Starting from this natural gift, people gradually developed their special aptitudes, until their rude improvisations gave birth to Poetry.

Poetry then diverged in two directions, according to the individual character of the writers. The graver spirits imitated noble actions, and the actions of good men. The more trivial sort imitated the actions of meaner persons, and at first composed satires, just as the graver kind composed hymns to the gods and praises of famous men. We cannot assign a poem of the satirical kind to any author earlier than Homer, though there were probably many such writers. From Homer onward, however, instances can be cited, such as his own Margites and other similar compositions. The appropriate meter was introduced here too. That is why the measure is still called the iambic or lampooning measure, since it was the one in which people lampooned one another. So the older poets were distinguished as writers of heroic verse or of lampooning verse.

In the serious style Homer stands out among poets, for he alone combined dramatic form with excellence of imitation. In the same way he was the first to lay down the main lines of Comedy, by dramatizing the ludicrous instead of writing personal satire. His Margites bears the same relation to Comedy that the Iliad and Odyssey bear to Tragedy. But when Tragedy and Comedy came to light, the two classes of poets still followed their natural bent. The lampooners became writers of Comedy, and Tragedians succeeded the Epic poets, since the drama was a larger and higher form of art.

Whether Tragedy has yet perfected its proper types or not, and whether it should be judged in itself or also in relation to the audience, is another question. Be that as it may, Tragedy, like Comedy, began as mere improvisation. Tragedy originated with the authors of the Dithyramb, and Comedy with the authors of the phallic songs, which are still in use in many of our cities. Tragedy advanced by slow degrees, and each new element that appeared was developed in turn. After many changes it found its natural form, and there it stopped.

Aeschylus first introduced a second actor. He reduced the importance of the Chorus and gave the leading part to the dialogue. Sophocles raised the number of actors to three and added scene-painting. It was also not until late that the short plot was given up for one of greater compass, and that the grotesque diction of the earlier satyric form gave way to the stately manner of Tragedy. Then the iambic measure replaced the trochaic tetrameter, which had been used originally when the poetry was of the Satyric order and had closer affinities with dancing. Once dialogue had come in, Nature herself found the appropriate measure. For the iambic is the most colloquial of all measures. We see this from the fact that conversational speech falls into iambic lines more often than into any other kind of verse. It rarely falls into hexameters, and only when we drop the colloquial intonation. The additional 'episodes' or acts, and the other accessories that tradition tells of, must be taken as already described, for it would doubtless be a large undertaking to discuss them in detail.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Comedy and epic compared with tragedy
paragraphs: Comedy, as we have said, is an imitation of characters of a lower type. They are not, however, bad in the full sense of the word, since the Ludicrous is merely a subdivision of the ugly. It consists in some defect or ugliness that is not painful or destructive. An obvious example is the comic mask, which is ugly and distorted but does not imply pain.

The successive changes through which Tragedy passed, and the authors of those changes, are well known. Comedy, by contrast, has had no history, because at first it was not treated seriously. It was late before the Archon granted a comic chorus to a poet; until then the performers were volunteers. Comedy had already taken definite shape by the time comic poets, distinctively so called, are heard of. Who gave it masks or prologues, or increased the number of actors, and other similar details, remain unknown. The plot originally came from Sicily. Among Athenian writers Crates was the first to give up the 'iambic' or lampooning form and to generalize his themes and plots.

Epic poetry agrees with Tragedy in being an imitation in verse of characters of a higher type. They differ in that Epic poetry admits only one kind of meter and is narrative in form. They differ, again, in length. Tragedy endeavors, as far as possible, to keep within a single revolution of the sun, or to exceed that limit only slightly, whereas the Epic action has no limits of time. This, then, is a second point of difference, although at first Tragedy was allowed the same freedom as Epic poetry.

Of their constituent parts, some are common to both, and some are peculiar to Tragedy. Therefore whoever knows what is good or bad Tragedy also knows about Epic poetry. All the elements of an Epic poem are found in Tragedy, but not all the elements of a Tragedy are found in the Epic poem.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Definition of tragedy and its parts
paragraphs: Poetry that imitates in hexameter verse, and Comedy, we will discuss later. For now let us turn to Tragedy and gather up its formal definition, which comes out of what we have already said.

Tragedy, then, is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions. By 'language embellished,' I mean language that has rhythm, 'harmony,' and song in it. By 'the several kinds in separate parts,' I mean that the play carries some parts by verse alone, and others by means of song as well.

Tragic imitation implies persons who act. So the first necessary consequence is that Spectacular equipment will be one part of Tragedy. Song and Diction come next, since these are what the imitation is made through. When I say 'Diction,' I mean simply the metrical arrangement of the words. 'Song' needs no explanation, because everyone knows what the term means.

Again, Tragedy imitates an action, and an action needs personal agents. These agents must have particular qualities of character and of thought, because those are what we use to describe the actions themselves. Thought and character are the two natural causes of actions, and success or failure in life rests on actions. Hence the Plot is the imitation of the action, and by plot I here mean the arrangement of the incidents. By Character I mean that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents. Thought is needed wherever someone proves a point or, it may be, states a general truth. Every Tragedy, therefore, must have six parts, and they determine its quality. These are Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song. Two of them are the medium of imitation, one is the manner, and three are the objects of imitation. The list is then complete. The poets have, we may say, made use of every one of these elements; indeed every play has Spectacular elements, and also Character, Plot, Diction, Song, and Thought.

Most important of all, however, is the structure of the incidents. Tragedy imitates not men but an action and a life. Life consists in action, and its end is a kind of action, not a quality. Men have their qualities from their character, but they are happy or unhappy because of their actions. So dramatic action is not performed to represent character; character comes in for the sake of the actions. Hence the incidents and the plot are the end of a tragedy, and the end is the chief thing of all. Again, a tragedy cannot exist without action, but it can exist without character. Most modern poets fail at rendering character, and poets in general often do. Painting shows the same thing, and it is where Zeuxis differs from Polygnotus: Polygnotus draws character well, but the style of Zeuxis lacks any ethical quality. Moreover, suppose you string together speeches that express character and are well finished in diction and thought. They will not achieve the essential tragic effect nearly as well as a play that falls short in these respects but has a plot and artistically constructed incidents. Besides, the most powerful means by which Tragedy stirs emotion, Peripeteia or Reversal of the Situation, and Recognition scenes, belong to the plot. There is a further proof. Beginners in the art manage polished diction and precise portrayal of character before they can construct a plot. Almost all the early poets were the same.

The Plot, then, is the first principle, and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy, and Character comes second. Painting offers a similar case. The most beautiful colors, laid on in confusion, will not please as much as a plain chalk outline of a portrait. So Tragedy is the imitation of an action, and it imitates the agents mainly for the sake of the action.

Third in order is Thought, that is, the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in the given circumstances. In speeches this is the task of the Political art and of the art of rhetoric. So the older poets made their characters speak the language of civic life, whereas the poets of our time make them speak like rhetoricians. Character is what reveals moral purpose, by showing what a man chooses or avoids. Speeches that do not make this clear, or in which the speaker chooses or avoids nothing at all, do not express character. Thought, on the other hand, appears where someone proves that something is or is not so, or states a general maxim.
Fourth among the elements we listed is Diction. By this I mean, as I have already said, the expression of the meaning in words, and its essence is the same in verse and in prose.
Among the remaining elements, Song holds the chief place among the embellishments.

The Spectacle does have an emotional attraction of its own, yet it is the least artistic of all the parts and has the least to do with the art of poetry. We may be sure that Tragedy has its power even without a performance and without actors. Besides, the art of the stage machinist matters more than the poet's art in producing spectacular effects.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Plot: magnitude and unity
paragraphs: Now that these principles are established, let us discuss how the Plot should properly be structured, since it is the first and most important thing in Tragedy.

According to our definition, Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is complete, and whole, and of a certain magnitude. I add 'magnitude' because a thing can be whole and yet lack magnitude. A whole has a beginning, a middle, and an end. A beginning does not itself have to follow anything by causal necessity, but something else naturally is or comes to be after it. An end is the opposite: it naturally follows something else, whether by necessity or as a rule, but nothing follows it. A middle follows something and is followed by something else. A well constructed plot, therefore, must not begin or end just anywhere. It must conform to these principles.

Again, a beautiful object, whether it is a living organism or any whole made up of parts, needs more than an orderly arrangement of its parts. It must also have a certain magnitude, because beauty depends on magnitude and order. This is why a very small animal organism cannot be beautiful: we see it in an almost imperceptible moment of time, so our view of it is confused. A vast one cannot be beautiful either. The eye cannot take it all in at once, so the spectator loses the unity and sense of the whole, as would happen with an animal a thousand miles long. Living bodies and organisms, then, need a certain magnitude, one that can easily be taken in at a single view. In the same way a plot needs a certain length, one that the memory can easily hold. Fixing the limit of length by the conditions of dramatic competition and of presenting the play to the senses is no part of artistic theory. If a hundred tragedies had to compete together, the water-clock would have set the length of the performance, and we are told this was in fact once done. The limit set by the nature of the drama itself is this: the longer the piece, the more beautiful it is because of its size, so long as the whole remains perspicuous. To define the matter roughly, we may say that the proper magnitude is whatever allows a sequence of events, according to the law of probability or necessity, to bring about a change from bad fortune to good, or from good fortune to bad.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — Unity of plot
paragraphs: Unity of plot does not consist, as some people think, in the Unity of the hero. The incidents in one man's life are infinitely various and cannot be reduced to unity, and in the same way one man performs many actions from which we cannot make one action. Hence, as it appears, all the poets who have composed a Heracleid, a Theseid, or other poems of the kind are in error. They imagine that because Heracles was one man, the story of Heracles must also be a unity. But Homer, who is of surpassing merit in everything else, seems to have seen the truth here too, whether through art or natural genius. In composing the Odyssey he did not include all the adventures of Odysseus, such as his wound on Parnassus or his feigned madness at the mustering of the host, incidents between which there was no necessary or probable connection. Instead he made the Odyssey, and likewise the Iliad, center on an action that is one in our sense of the word. In the other imitative arts, the imitation is one when the object imitated is one. In the same way the plot, being an imitation of an action, must imitate one action, and a whole one. The parts must be so joined structurally that if any one of them is displaced or removed, the whole is disjointed and disturbed. For a thing whose presence or absence makes no visible difference is not an organic part of the whole.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — Poetry vs history
paragraphs: What has been said also makes it evident that the poet's function is not to relate what has happened but what may happen, meaning what is possible according to the law of probability or necessity. Poet and historian are not distinguished by writing verse or prose. Herodotus could be put into verse, and his work would be no less a species of history in meter than without it. The real difference is that the historian relates what has happened and the poet what may happen. For this reason poetry is more philosophical and a higher thing than history: poetry tends to express the universal, and history the particular. By the universal I mean the kinds of things that a person of a certain type will say or do on occasion, according to the law of probability or necessity. Poetry aims at this universality when it attaches names to its personages. The particular is, for example, what Alcibiades did or suffered. Comedy already makes this apparent. There the poet first constructs the plot on the lines of probability and then inserts characteristic names, unlike the lampooners, who write about particular individuals. Tragedians, however, still keep to real names. The reason is that what is possible is credible. We are not at once sure that what has not happened is possible, whereas what has happened is manifestly possible, for otherwise it would not have happened. Even so, in some tragedies only one or two of the names are well known and the others are made up. In others none is well known, as in Agathon's Antheus, where incidents and names are alike invented, and still the play pleases just as much. So we must not cling at all costs to the received legends that Tragedy usually takes as its subjects. It would be absurd to try, since even the known subjects are known only to a few, and yet they please everyone. It follows plainly that the poet or 'maker' should be a maker of plots rather than of verses. He is a poet because he imitates, and what he imitates are actions. Even if he happens to take an historical subject, he is still a poet. Nothing prevents some events that really happened from conforming to the law of the probable and possible, and because they have that quality he is their poet or maker.

The epeisodic are the worst of all plots and actions. By an 'epeisodic' plot I mean one in which the episodes or acts follow one another with no probable or necessary sequence. Bad poets write such plays because they are at fault, and good poets write them to please the players. Since they write show pieces for competition, they stretch the plot beyond what it can bear, and are often forced to break its natural continuity.

Tragedy, however, imitates not only a complete action but also events that inspire fear or pity. The best way to produce this effect is for the events to come as a surprise. The effect is stronger when, at the same time, they follow from one another as cause and effect. The tragic wonder is then greater than if the events happened by themselves or by accident, since even coincidences strike us most when they look designed. An instance is the statue of Mitys at Argos, which fell on the man who had murdered Mitys, as he watched a festival, and killed him. Such events do not seem to be mere chance. Plots built on these principles are therefore necessarily the best.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — Simple and complex plots
paragraphs: Some plots are Simple and others Complex. The actions of real life, which plots imitate, plainly divide in the same way. When an action is one and continuous in the sense defined above, and the change of fortune comes about without Reversal of the Situation and without Recognition, I call it Simple.

A Complex action is one where the change of fortune comes with Reversal, or with Recognition, or with both. These should grow out of the internal structure of the plot, so that what follows is the necessary or probable result of what came before. It makes all the difference whether a given event is a case of propter hoc or post hoc.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Reversal, recognition, and suffering
paragraphs: Reversal of the Situation is a change by which the action turns into its opposite, and this is always subject to our rule of probability or necessity. In the Oedipus, for example, the messenger arrives to cheer Oedipus and to free him from his fears about his mother. By revealing who Oedipus is, he produces the opposite effect. Again, in the Lynceus, Lynceus is being led off to his death, with Danaus going along to kill him. But the earlier incidents lead to the result that Danaus is killed and Lynceus saved. Recognition, as its name indicates, is a change from ignorance to knowledge, and it produces love or hate between the persons whom the poet has destined for good or bad fortune. The best form of recognition occurs together with a Reversal of the Situation, as in the Oedipus. There are indeed other forms. Even inanimate things of the most trivial kind may in a sense be objects of recognition. We may also recognize or discover whether a person has done something or not. But the recognition that is most closely tied to the plot and the action is, as we have said, the recognition of persons. When this is combined with Reversal, it will produce either pity or fear, and these are the effects of the actions that, by our definition, Tragedy represents. Moreover, the issues of good or bad fortune will turn on such situations. Recognition is between persons, so it may be that only one of them is recognized by the other, when the other is already known. Or it may be necessary for the recognition to go both ways. Thus the sending of the letter reveals Iphigenia to Orestes, but a second act of recognition is needed to make Orestes known to Iphigenia.

Two parts of the Plot, then, Reversal of the Situation and Recognition, depend on surprises. A third part is the Scene of Suffering. The Scene of Suffering is a destructive or painful action, such as death on the stage, bodily agony, wounds and the like.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Quantitative parts of tragedy
paragraphs: [We have already mentioned the parts of Tragedy that must be treated as elements of the whole. We now come to the quantitative parts, the separate parts into which Tragedy is divided, namely Prologue, Episode, Exode, and Choric song, this last being divided into Parode and Stasimon. These are common to all plays. Peculiar to some are the songs of actors from the stage and the Commoi.

The Prologue is the entire part of a tragedy that comes before the Parode of the Chorus. The Episode is the entire part of a tragedy that lies between complete choric songs. The Exode is the entire part of a tragedy after which there is no choric song. Of the Choric part, the Parode is the first undivided utterance of the Chorus. The Stasimon is a Choric ode without anapaests or trochaic tetrameters. The Commos is a joint lamentation of Chorus and actors. We have already mentioned the parts of Tragedy that must be treated as elements of the whole. The quantitative parts, the separate parts into which it is divided, are listed here.]

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — The tragic plot
paragraphs: Following on from what has been said, we must next consider what the poet should aim at and what he should avoid when he constructs his plots. We must also ask by what means Tragedy will produce its specific effect.

As we have seen, a perfect tragedy should be built on the complex plan, not the simple. It should also imitate actions that arouse pity and fear, for that is the distinctive mark of tragic imitation. The first thing that follows is that we must not see a virtuous man pass from prosperity to adversity. This moves neither pity nor fear; it only shocks us. Nor must we see a bad man pass from adversity to prosperity. Nothing could be more foreign to the spirit of Tragedy. Such a plot has not a single tragic quality: it does not satisfy the moral sense, and it arouses neither pity nor fear. Nor again should we see the utter villain fall. A plot like that would doubtless satisfy the moral sense, but it would arouse neither pity nor fear, since pity is aroused by undeserved misfortune, and fear by the misfortune of a man like ourselves. Such an event, then, will be neither pitiful nor terrible. What remains is the character between these extremes. This is a man who is not eminently good and just, and whose misfortune comes upon him not through vice or depravity but through some error or frailty. He must also be a man of great renown and prosperity, a figure such as Oedipus, Thyestes, or other illustrious men of such families.

A well constructed plot should therefore have a single issue, not a double one as some maintain. The change of fortune should go not from bad to good but the other way, from good to bad. It should result not from vice but from some great error or frailty, in a character of the kind we have described, or one better rather than worse. The practice of the stage supports our view. At first the poets told whatever legend came to hand. Now the best tragedies are founded on the stories of a few houses: the fortunes of Alcmaeon, Oedipus, Orestes, Meleager, Thyestes, Telephus, and the rest who have done or suffered something terrible. To be perfect by the rules of art, then, a tragedy should have this construction. So those who criticize Euripides for following this principle in his plays, many of which end unhappily, are in error. As we have said, this is the right ending. The best proof is that on the stage and in dramatic competition such plays, when well worked out, have the most tragic effect. And although Euripides may be faulty in the overall management of his subject, he is still felt to be the most tragic of the poets.

The kind of tragedy that some people rank first comes only second. It has a double thread of plot, as the Odyssey does, and ends in opposite ways for the good and for the bad. People account it the best because of the weakness of the spectators, since the poet writes to suit the wishes of his audience. But the pleasure it gives is not the true tragic pleasure. It belongs rather to Comedy. There the deadliest enemies of the piece, such as Orestes and Aegisthus, walk off the stage as friends at the end, and nobody kills or is killed.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Pity and fear from incidents
paragraphs: Fear and pity can be aroused by spectacular means, but they can also result from the inner structure of the piece. That is the better way, and it marks a superior poet. The plot ought to be built so that someone who only hears the tale, without seeing anything, will shudder with horror and melt with pity at what happens. This is the impression we should get from hearing the story of the Oedipus. Producing this effect by spectacle alone is a less artistic method and relies on outside aids. Some use spectacular means to create a sense not of the terrible but only of the monstrous. They are strangers to the purpose of Tragedy, for we must not ask Tragedy for every kind of pleasure, only for the pleasure proper to it. The pleasure the poet should provide is the one that comes from pity and fear through imitation. So it is evident that this quality must be built into the incidents.
Let us then decide which circumstances strike us as terrible or pitiful.

Actions that can have this effect must take place between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent to one another. When an enemy kills an enemy, nothing in the act or in the intention excites pity, except in so far as the suffering itself is pitiful. The same goes for indifferent persons. The poet should look instead for situations where the tragic incident occurs between people who are near or dear to one another. Examples are a brother who kills, or intends to kill, a brother, a son his father, a mother her son, a son his mother, or any other deed of that kind. The poet may not, indeed, destroy the framework of the received legends. He cannot change the fact, for instance, that Orestes killed Clytemnestra and Alcmaeon killed Eriphyle. But he ought to show invention of his own and handle the traditional material with skill. Let us explain more clearly what we mean by skillful handling.

The action may be done consciously and with knowledge of the persons, as the older poets did it. This is how Euripides too makes Medea kill her children. Or the horrible deed may be done in ignorance, with the tie of kinship or friendship discovered afterwards. The Oedipus of Sophocles is an example. In that play the incident lies outside the drama proper, but sometimes it falls within the action of the play, as in the Alcmaeon of Astydamas, or Telegonus in the Wounded Odysseus. There is also a third case: <to be about to act with knowledge of the persons and then not to act. The fourth case is> when someone is about to do an irreparable deed through ignorance and makes the discovery before he does it. These are the only possible ways, for the deed must be either done or not done, and either knowingly or unknowingly. Of all these ways, the worst is to be about to act knowing the persons and then not to act. It is shocking without being tragic, since no disaster follows. For that reason it is never, or very rarely, found in poetry. One instance is in the Antigone, where Haemon threatens to kill Creon. The next way, which is better, is for the deed to be carried out. Better still is for it to be carried out in ignorance and for the discovery to come afterwards. Then there is nothing to shock us, and the discovery has a startling effect. The last case is the best. In the Cresphontes, for example, Merope is about to kill her son but recognizes who he is and spares his life. In the Iphigenia, likewise, the sister recognizes the brother just in time. And in the Helle the son recognizes his mother just as he is about to give her up. This, as already observed, is why only a few families provide the subjects of tragedy. It was not art but happy chance that led the poets, as they searched for subjects, to give their plots the tragic quality. So they have to turn to those houses whose history holds moving incidents like these.
This is enough on the structure of the incidents and the right kind of plot.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Character in tragedy
paragraphs: There are four things to aim at in Character. First, and most important, it must be good. Any speech or action that shows moral purpose of any kind will express character, and the character will be good if the purpose is good. This rule applies within each class of persons. Even a woman may be good, and so may a slave, though the woman may be said to be an inferior being, and the slave altogether worthless. The second thing to aim at is propriety. There is a type of manly valor, but valor in a woman, or unscrupulous cleverness, is inappropriate. Third, character must be true to life, which is a different matter from goodness and propriety as described here. The fourth point is consistency. Even if the person imitated, who suggested the type, is inconsistent, he must still be consistently inconsistent. For an example of motiveless degradation of character we have Menelaus in the Orestes; for character that is indecorous and inappropriate, the lament of Odysseus in the Scylla and the speech of Melanippe; for inconsistency, the Iphigenia at Aulis — for Iphigenia the suppliant in no way resembles her later self.

The poet should always aim at the necessary or the probable — in drawing character just as in building the structure of the plot. A person of a given character should speak or act in a given way because necessity or probability requires it, and one event should follow another by the same necessary or probable sequence. It is therefore evident that the unraveling of a plot, like the complication, has to grow out of the plot itself. The 'Deus ex Machina' must not bring it about — as happens in the Medea, or in the Return of the Greeks in the Iliad. The 'Deus ex Machina' should be used only for events outside the drama: those that happened before it or will happen after it, which no human being could know and which therefore have to be reported or foretold, since we credit the gods with seeing all things. Nothing irrational may occur within the action. If the irrational cannot be avoided, it should stay outside the scope of the tragedy. The irrational element in the Oedipus of Sophocles is of this kind.

Again, Tragedy imitates persons who are above the common level, so the poet should follow good portrait-painters. These painters keep the distinctive form of the original, yet paint a likeness that is both true to life and more beautiful. The poet does the same when he represents men who are irascible or indolent or who have other defects of character: he should preserve the type and yet ennoble it. Achilles, as Agathon and Homer portray him, is an instance.

These are the rules the poet should observe. He should also not neglect the appeals to the senses that go along with poetry, though they are not among its essentials; here too much error is possible. But I have said enough about this in our published treatises.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — Forms of recognition
paragraphs: We have already explained what Recognition is. Now we will go through its kinds.

The first kind is the least artistic, and poverty of wit makes it the one most often used: recognition by signs. Some signs are congenital — such as 'the spear which the earth-born race bear on their bodies,' or the stars Carcinus introduced in his Thyestes. Others are acquired after birth. Some of these are marks on the body, such as scars; others are external tokens, such as necklaces, or the little ark in the Tyro, by which the discovery is made. Even these can be used with more or less skill. When Odysseus is recognized by his scar, for instance, the nurse makes the discovery in one way and the swineherds in another. Tokens used expressly to prove something — and indeed any formal proof, with tokens or without — make a less artistic recognition. A better kind is the one that comes about through a turn of incident, as in the Bath Scene in the Odyssey.

Next come the recognitions that the poet invents at will, which lack art for that reason. In the Iphigenia, for example, Orestes reveals that he is Orestes. Iphigenia makes herself known by the letter, but Orestes speaks for himself and says what the poet wants, not what the plot requires. This comes close to the fault just mentioned, since Orestes might as well have brought tokens with him. The 'voice of the shuttle' in the Tereus of Sophocles is another similar case.

The third kind depends on memory, when the sight of something awakens a feeling. In the Cyprians of Dicaeogenes the hero bursts into tears when he sees the picture; in the 'Lay of Alcinous' Odysseus hears the minstrel playing the lyre, remembers the past and weeps; and so the recognition follows.

The fourth kind proceeds by reasoning. In the Choephori, for example: 'Some one resembling me has come: no one resembles me but Orestes: therefore Orestes has come.' Iphigenia's discovery in the play of Polyidus the Sophist is of the same sort. It was natural for Orestes to reflect, 'So I too must die at the altar like my sister.' In the Tydeus of Theodectes likewise, the father says, 'I came to find my son, and I lose my own life.' And in the Phineidae the women, when they saw the place, inferred their fate: 'Here we are doomed to die, for here we were cast forth.' There is also a composite kind of recognition, in which one of the characters draws a false inference, as in the Odysseus Disguised as a Messenger. A said <that no one else was able to bend the bow;... hence B (the disguised Odysseus) imagined that A would> recognise the bow which, in fact, he had not seen. To bring about a recognition by this means, through the expectation that A would recognize the bow, is false inference.

Of all recognitions, however, the best arises from the incidents themselves, when the startling discovery comes through natural means. The recognition in the Oedipus of Sophocles is of this kind, and so is the one in the Iphigenia, for it was natural that Iphigenia would want to send a letter. Only these recognitions need no artificial help from tokens or amulets. Recognitions by a process of reasoning come next.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — Practical advice for the poet
paragraphs: When the poet constructs the plot and works it out with the proper diction, he should put the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes. He will then see everything with the utmost vividness, as though he were a spectator of the action, and so find what suits it and be least likely to miss inconsistencies. The fault found in Carcinus shows why such a rule is needed. Amphiaraus was on his way from the temple, a fact that escaped a man who did not picture the situation. On the stage the piece failed, because the audience was offended at the oversight.

Again, the poet should work out his play with the gestures that suit it, as far as he is able. People who actually feel an emotion are the most convincing, through natural sympathy with the characters they represent; someone who is agitated storms, and someone who is angry rages, with the most life-like reality. Hence poetry calls for either a happy gift of nature or a strain of madness. With the first, a man can take on the mold of any character; with the second, he is lifted out of his proper self.

As for the story, whether the poet takes it ready made or constructs it himself, he should first sketch its general outline, and only then fill in the episodes and expand the details. The Iphigenia can show how the general plan works. A young girl is sacrificed and mysteriously vanishes from the sight of those who sacrificed her. She is carried to another country, where the custom is to offer all strangers to the goddess, and she is appointed to this ministry. Some time later her own brother happens to arrive. That the oracle ordered him to go there, for some reason, lies outside the general plan of the play; and the purpose of his coming is likewise outside the action proper. At any rate he arrives and is seized, and just as he is about to be sacrificed he reveals who he is. He may do so in the manner of Euripides or in that of Polyidus, in whose play he exclaims, very naturally — 'So it was not my sister only, but I too, who was doomed to be sacrificed'; and by that remark he is saved.

Once the names are given, what remains is to fill in the episodes. We must make sure that they are relevant to the action. In Orestes' case, for instance, there is the madness that led to his capture, and his deliverance through the purificatory rite. In drama the episodes are short; in Epic poetry they are what give the work its length. The story of the Odyssey, for example, can be told in a few words. A man is away from home for many years, watched jealously by Poseidon and left desolate. Meanwhile his house is in a wretched state: suitors are wasting his substance and plotting against his son. At last he arrives himself, tempest-tossed; he makes himself known to certain people, attacks the suitors with his own hand, and survives while he destroys them. That is the essence of the plot; the rest is episode.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — Complication and unraveling
paragraphs: Every tragedy has two parts — Complication and Unraveling or Denouement. The Complication is formed from incidents extraneous to the action, often combined with a portion of the action proper; the rest is the Unraveling. By the Complication I mean everything from the beginning of the action up to the point that marks the turn to good or bad fortune, and by the Unraveling everything from the start of the change to the end. In the Lynceus of Theodectes, for instance, the Complication consists of the incidents presupposed in the drama, the seizure of the child, and then again. The Unraveling runs from the accusation of murder to the end.

Tragedy has four kinds: the Complex, which depends entirely on Reversal of the Situation and Recognition; the Pathetic (where the motive is passion), such as the tragedies on Ajax and Ixion; the Ethical (where the motives are ethical), such as the Phthiotides and the Peleus; and, fourth, the Simple <We here exclude the purely spectacular element>, of which the Phorcides, the Prometheus, and scenes laid in Hades are examples. The poet should try, if he can, to combine all the poetic elements; failing that, he should combine the greatest number and the most important, especially given the fault-finding criticism of the day. Good poets have so far each excelled in his own branch, and now the critics expect a single man to surpass all of them in each one's own line of excellence.

To decide whether two tragedies are the same or different, the best test is the plot. They are the same when their Complication and Unraveling are the same. Many poets tie the knot well and unravel it badly. A poet should always master both arts.

Again, the poet should remember what has often been said: he should not make a Tragedy out of an Epic structure — by an Epic structure I mean one with a multiplicity of plots — as if, for example, you tried to make a tragedy of the entire story of the Iliad. In the Epic poem each part takes its proper magnitude because of the poem's length; in the drama the result is far from what the poet expects. The proof is that poets who dramatized the whole Fall of Troy rather than choosing portions, as Euripides did, or who took the whole tale of Niobe instead of part of it, as Aeschylus did, either fail completely or do poorly on the stage. Even Agathon has failed from this one defect alone. In his Reversals of the Situation, however, he shows marvelous skill in aiming at the popular taste — at a tragic effect that satisfies the moral sense. That effect arises when a clever rogue like Sisyphus is outwitted, or a brave villain is defeated. Such an event is probable in Agathon's sense of the word: 'it is probable,' he says, 'that many things should happen contrary to probability.'

The Chorus too should be treated as one of the actors. It should be an integral part of the whole and take part in the action, as in Sophocles and not as in Euripides. In the later poets, the choral songs have no more to do with the subject of the piece than with that of any other tragedy. They are therefore sung as mere interludes, a practice Agathon began. Yet what difference is there between singing such interludes and transferring a speech, or even a whole act, from one play to another?

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — Thought and diction
paragraphs: Diction and Thought remain to be discussed, since we have already treated the other parts of Tragedy. For Thought we may rely on what the Rhetoric says, because that inquiry is where the subject properly belongs. Thought covers every effect that has to be produced by speech. Its subdivisions are proof and refutation; the arousing of feelings such as pity, fear, anger, and the like; and the suggestion of importance or its opposite. Plainly the dramatic incidents must be handled from the same points of view as the dramatic speeches, whenever the aim is to produce a sense of pity, fear, importance, or probability. There is only one difference: the incidents should speak for themselves without verbal exposition, while the effects sought in speech must be produced by the speaker and by means of his speech. For what would be a speaker's business if the Thought showed itself quite apart from what he says?

Now for Diction. One branch of this inquiry deals with the Modes of Utterance. That body of knowledge, however, belongs to the art of Delivery and to its masters. It covers, for example, what a command is, a prayer, a statement, a threat, a question, an answer, and so on. Whether the poet knows these things or not, his art incurs no serious censure. For who can accept the fault that Protagoras charges against Homer: that in the words 'Sing, goddess, of the wrath' he gives a command while believing he utters a prayer? Telling someone to do a thing or not to do it is, Protagoras says, a command. We may therefore set this aside as belonging to another art and not to poetry.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 — Parts of language
paragraphs: [Language in general has the following parts: Letter, Syllable, Connecting word, Noun, Verb, Inflexion or Case, Sentence or Phrase.

A Letter is an indivisible sound — yet not every such sound, but only one that can form part of a group of sounds. For even animals utter indivisible sounds, and I do not call any of these a letter. The sound I mean may be a vowel, a semi-vowel, or a mute. A vowel is a sound that is audible without any impact of tongue or lip. A semi-vowel is a sound that is audible with such an impact, as S and R. A mute is a sound that with such an impact has no sound by itself, but becomes audible when joined to a vowel sound, as G and D. These are distinguished by the shape the mouth takes and the place where they are produced; by whether they are aspirated or smooth, long or short; and by whether they are acute, grave, or of an intermediate tone. The detailed study of these points belongs to the writers on meter.

A Syllable is a non-significant sound composed of a mute and a vowel: GR without A is a syllable, and so is GR with A — GRA. But the investigation of these differences also belongs to the science of meter.

A Connecting word is a non-significant sound. It neither causes nor prevents the union of many sounds into one significant sound, and it may stand at either end of a sentence or in the middle. Or it is a non-significant sound that can make one significant sound out of several that are each significant — as {alpha mu theta iota}, {pi epsilon rho iota}, and the like. Or it is a non-significant sound that marks the start, end, or division of a sentence, though it cannot correctly stand alone at the start of a sentence — as {mu epsilon nu}, {eta tau omicron iota}, {delta epsilon}.

A Noun is a composite significant sound that does not mark time and has no part that is significant in itself. In double or compound words we do not treat the separate parts as significant in themselves. In Theodorus, 'god-given,' for example, the {delta omega rho omicron nu} or 'gift' has no significance by itself.

A Verb is also a composite significant sound, but it marks time, and like the noun it has no part that is significant in itself. 'Man' or 'white' does not express the idea of 'when,' whereas 'he walks' or 'he has walked' does connote time, present or past.

Inflexion belongs to the noun and the verb alike. It expresses the relation 'of,' 'to,' or the like; or number, one or many, as 'man' or 'men'; or the modes or tones of actual delivery, such as a question or a command. 'Did he go?' and 'go' are verbal inflexions of this kind.

A Sentence or Phrase is a composite significant sound of which at least some parts are significant in themselves. Not every such group of words is made of verbs and nouns — 'the definition of man,' for instance — since it may do without even the verb. But it will always have some significant part, as 'in walking' or 'Cleon son of Cleon.' A sentence or phrase can be a unity in two ways: it may signify one thing, or it may link several parts together. The Iliad is one by the linking of parts, the definition of man by the unity of the thing it signifies.]

chapters.title: Chapter 21 — Kinds of words
paragraphs: Words are either simple or double. By simple I mean those made of non-significant elements, such as {gamma eta}. By double or compound I mean those made either of a significant and a non-significant element (though within the whole word no element is significant), or of elements that are both significant. A word may also be triple, quadruple, or multiple in form, like so many Massilian expressions, e.g. 'Hermo-caico-xanthus who prayed to Father Zeus.'
Every word is one of these: current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, or altered.

By a current or proper word I mean one in general use among a people; by a strange word, one used in another country. Obviously, then, one and the same word can be both strange and current, though not for the same people. The word {sigma iota gamma upsilon nu omicron nu}, 'lance,' is a current word for the Cyprians and a strange one for us.

Metaphor is the transfer of an alien name to something, either from genus to species, from species to genus, from species to species, or by analogy, which means proportion. An example of genus to species is 'There lies my ship,' for lying at anchor is one species of lying. An example of species to genus is 'Verily ten thousand noble deeds hath Odysseus wrought,' where ten thousand, a species of large number, is used for a large number in general. From species to species: 'With blade of bronze drew away the life,' and 'Cleft the water with the vessel of unyielding bronze.' Here {alpha rho upsilon rho alpha iota}, 'to draw away,' is used for {tau alpha mu epsilon iota nu}, 'to cleave,' and {tau alpha mu epsilon iota nu} again for {alpha rho upsilon alpha iota}, since each is a species of taking away. Analogy or proportion holds when the second term is to the first as the fourth is to the third. Then we may use the fourth for the second, or the second for the fourth. Sometimes we also qualify the metaphor by adding the term to which the proper word is related. The cup is to Dionysus as the shield is to Ares, so the cup may be called 'the shield of Dionysus,' and the shield 'the cup of Ares.' Likewise, old age is to life as evening is to day, so evening may be called 'the old age of the day,' and old age 'the evening of life,' or, in the phrase of Empedocles, 'life's setting sun.' Sometimes there is no existing word for one of the terms of the proportion, yet the metaphor can still be used. To scatter seed is called sowing, for instance, but the sun's scattering of his rays has no name. Still, this action is to the sun as sowing is to the seed, and hence the poet says 'sowing the god-created light.' There is another way to use this kind of metaphor: we apply an alien term and then deny it one of its proper attributes, as if we called the shield not 'the cup of Ares' but 'the wineless cup.'
{An ornamental word...}

A newly-coined word has never been used even locally; the poet adopts it himself. Some such words seem to exist, such as {epsilon rho nu upsilon gamma epsilon sigma}, 'sprouters,' for {kappa epsilon rho alpha tau alpha}, 'horns,' and {alpha rho eta tau eta rho}, 'supplicator,' for {iota epsilon rho epsilon upsilon sigma}, 'priest.'

A word is lengthened if its own vowel is replaced by a longer one or if a syllable is inserted; it is contracted if part of it is removed. Examples of lengthening are {pi omicron lambda eta omicron sigma} for {pi omicron lambda epsilon omega sigma}, and {Pi eta lambda eta iota alpha delta epsilon omega} for {Pi eta lambda epsilon iota delta omicron upsilon}; examples of contraction are {kappa rho iota}, {delta omega}, and {omicron psi}, as in {mu iota alpha / gamma iota nu epsilon tau alpha iota / alpha mu phi omicron tau episilon rho omega nu / omicron psi}.

A word is altered when part of the ordinary form is kept and part is recast, as in {delta epsilon xi iota-tau epsilon rho omicron nu / kappa alpha tau alpha / mu alpha zeta omicron nu}, where {delta epsilon xi iota tau epsilon rho omicron nu} stands for {delta epsilon xi iota omicron nu}.

[Nouns themselves are masculine, feminine, or neuter. The masculine ones end in {nu}, {rho}, {sigma}, or in a letter compounded with {sigma} — these being two, and {xi}. The feminine ones end in vowels that are always long, namely {eta} and {omega}, and, among the vowels that can be lengthened, in {alpha}. So masculine and feminine nouns end in the same number of letters, since {psi} and {xi} count as endings in {sigma}. No noun ends in a mute or in a vowel short by nature. Only three end in {iota} — {mu eta lambda iota}, {kappa omicron mu mu iota}, {pi epsilon pi epsilon rho iota} — and five end in {upsilon}. Neuter nouns end in the two vowels just named, and also in {nu} and {sigma}.]

chapters.title: Chapter 22 — Diction
paragraphs: Style is perfect when it is clear without being mean. A style that uses only current or proper words is the clearest, but it is mean — as the poetry of Cleophon and of Sthenelus shows. Diction becomes lofty and rises above the commonplace when it uses unusual words. By unusual I mean strange (or rare) words, metaphors, lengthened forms — anything, in short, that departs from the normal idiom. But a style made wholly of such words is a riddle or a jargon: a riddle if it consists of metaphors, a jargon if it consists of strange (or rare) words. The essence of a riddle is to express true facts through impossible combinations. Ordinary words cannot be arranged to do that, but metaphor can. This is such a riddle: 'A man I saw who on another man had glued the bronze by aid of fire,' and others of the same kind. A diction made of strange (or rare) terms is a jargon. Style therefore needs a certain admixture of these elements: the strange (or rare) word, the metaphorical, the ornamental, and the other kinds mentioned above lift it above the commonplace and mean, while proper words make it clear. Nothing helps more, though, to give a clear diction that is not commonplace than lengthening, contracting, and altering words. By departing from the normal idiom in exceptional cases the language gains distinction, and by partly following usage it stays clear. So the critics who censure these licenses of speech and ridicule the author are in error. Eucleides the elder, for instance, declared that being a poet would be easy if you could lengthen syllables at will. He caricatured the practice in the very form of his diction, as in the verse: '{Epsilon pi iota chi alpha rho eta nu / epsilon iota delta omicron nu / Mu alpha rho alpha theta omega nu alpha delta epsilon / Beta alpha delta iota zeta omicron nu tau alpha}, or, {omicron upsilon kappa / alpha nu / gamma / epsilon rho alpha mu epsilon nu omicron sigma / tau omicron nu / epsilon kappa epsilon iota nu omicron upsilon /epsilon lambda lambda epsilon beta omicron rho omicron nu}. To use such license obtrusively is no doubt grotesque, but moderation is needed in every mode of poetic diction. Metaphors, strange (or rare) words, and any similar forms of speech would have the same effect if they were used without propriety and with the express purpose of being ludicrous. Epic poetry shows how great a difference the appropriate use of lengthening makes: insert the ordinary forms into the verse and you will see. The same holds if we replace a strange (or rare) word, a metaphor, or any similar expression with the current or proper term; the truth of our observation will then be plain. Aeschylus and Euripides, for example, each composed the same iambic line. Euripides changed a single word, putting the rarer term in place of the ordinary one, and one verse looks beautiful while the other looks trivial. Aeschylus in his Philoctetes says: {Phi alpha gamma epsilon delta alpha iota nu alpha / delta / eta / mu omicron upsilon / sigma alpha rho kappa alpha sigma / epsilon rho theta iota epsilon iota / pi omicron delta omicron sigma}.

Euripides puts {Theta omicron iota nu alpha tau alpha iota} 'feasts on' in place of {epsilon sigma theta iota epsilon iota} 'feeds on.' Again, in the line {nu upsilon nu / delta epsilon / mu /epsilon omega nu / omicron lambda iota gamma iota gamma upsilon sigma / tau epsilon / kappa alpha iota / omicron upsilon tau iota delta alpha nu omicron sigma / kappa alpha iota / alpha epsilon iota kappa eta sigma), the difference will be felt if we substitute the common words {nu upsilon nu / delta epsilon / mu / epsilon omega nu / mu iota kappa rho omicron sigma / tau epsilon / kappa alpha iota / alpha rho theta epsilon nu iota kappa omicron sigma / kappa alpha iota / alpha epsilon iota delta gamma sigma}. Or suppose that for the line {delta iota phi rho omicron nu / alpha epsilon iota kappa epsilon lambda iota omicron nu / kappa alpha tau alpha theta epsilon iota sigma / omicron lambda iota gamma eta nu / tau epsilon / tau rho alpha pi epsilon iota sigma / omicron lambda iota gamma eta nu / tau epsilon / tau rho alpha pi epsilon zeta alpha nu,} we read {delta iota phi rho omicron nu / mu omicron chi theta eta rho omicron nu / kappa alpha tau alpha theta epsilon iota sigma / mu iota kappa rho alpha nu / tau epsilon / tau rho alpha pi epsilon zeta alpha nu}.
Or, for {eta iota omicron nu epsilon sigma / beta omicron omicron omega rho iota nu, eta iota omicron nu epsilon sigma kappa rho alpha zeta omicron upsilon rho iota nu}

Again, Ariphrades ridiculed the tragedians for using phrases that no one would use in ordinary speech, such as {delta omega mu alpha tau omega nu / alpha pi omicron} instead of {alpha pi omicron / delta omega mu alpha tau omega nu}, {rho epsilon theta epsilon nu}, {epsilon gamma omega / delta epsilon / nu iota nu}, and {Alpha chi iota lambda lambda epsilon omega sigma / pi epsilon rho iota} instead of {pi epsilon rho iota / 'Alpha chi iota lambda lambda epsilon omega sigma}, and the like. It is precisely because such phrases are not part of the current idiom that they give distinction to the style. This, however, he failed to see.

It matters greatly to observe propriety in all these modes of expression, in compound words and strange (or rare) words and the rest. But by far the greatest thing is to have a command of metaphor. No one else can teach this; it is a mark of genius, since making good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances.

Of the various kinds of words, compound ones suit Dithyrambs best, rare words suit heroic poetry, and metaphors suit iambic. In heroic poetry all these kinds are useful. But iambic verse imitates familiar speech as closely as it can, so the words that suit it best are those found even in prose: the current or proper, the metaphorical, and the ornamental.
Concerning Tragedy and imitation by means of action, this may suffice.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 — Epic structure
paragraphs: Now take poetic imitation that is narrative in form and uses a single meter. Its plot, plainly, ought to be built on dramatic principles, as in a tragedy. Its subject should be a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end, so that it resembles a living organism in all its unity and gives the pleasure proper to it. Its structure will differ from that of historical compositions, which must present not a single action but a single period — everything that happened in it to one person or to many, however loosely connected the events. The sea-fight at Salamis and the battle with the Carthaginians in Sicily took place at the same time yet led to no single result; likewise in a sequence of events one thing sometimes follows another without producing any single result. Most poets, we may say, work this way. Here again, as already noted, the transcendent excellence of Homer is manifest. Though the war of Troy had a beginning and an end, he never attempts to make the whole of it the subject of his poem. That would have been too vast a theme, not easily taken in at a single view; and if he had kept it within moderate limits, the variety of incidents must have over-complicated it. As it is, he takes a single portion and uses many events from the general story of the war as episodes — such as the Catalogue of the ships and others — and so diversifies the poem. All other poets take a single hero, a single period, or an action that is single but has many parts. The author of the Cypria and of the Little Iliad did this. For that reason the Iliad and the Odyssey each supply the subject of one tragedy, or at most two, whereas the Cypria supplies materials for many and the Little Iliad for eight — the Award of the Arms, the Philoctetes, the Neoptolemus, the Eurypylus, the Mendicant Odysseus, the Laconian Women, the Fall of Ilium, the Departure of the Fleet.

chapters.title: Chapter 24 — Epic compared with tragedy
paragraphs: Epic poetry, again, must have as many kinds as Tragedy: it must be simple, complex, 'ethical,' or 'pathetic.' Its parts are the same too, apart from song and spectacle, since it needs Reversals of the Situation, Recognitions, and Scenes of Suffering. Its thoughts and diction must also be artistic. In all of this Homer is our earliest and sufficient model. Each of his poems, in fact, has a twofold character: the Iliad is simple and 'pathetic' at once, while the Odyssey is complex (Recognition scenes run all through it) and 'ethical' at the same time. And in diction and thought both are supreme.

Epic poetry differs from Tragedy in the scale of its construction and in its meter. On scale or length we have already set an adequate limit: the beginning and the end must be able to be taken in at a single view. Poems shorter than the old epics, and equal in length to the group of tragedies given at one sitting, would meet this condition.

Yet Epic poetry has a great — a special — capacity for extending its dimensions, and the reason is plain. Tragedy cannot imitate several lines of action going on at the same time; it has to keep to the action on the stage and to what the players do. Epic poetry is narrative, so it can present many events taking place simultaneously, and if they are relevant to the subject they add mass and dignity to the poem. This is an advantage for the Epic: it adds grandeur, diverts the hearer's mind, and relieves the story with varied episodes. Sameness of incident soon causes satiety, and it is what makes tragedies fail on the stage.

As for meter, the heroic measure has proved its fitness by experience. A narrative poem composed in any other meter, or in many, would now seem incongruous. Of all measures the heroic is the stateliest and most massive, and so it is the most ready to admit rare words and metaphors — another respect in which the narrative form of imitation stands alone. The iambic and the trochaic tetrameter, by contrast, are stirring measures: the trochaic is akin to dancing, the iambic expresses action. It would be more absurd still to mix different meters, as Chaeremon did. This is why no one has composed a poem on a great scale in anything but heroic verse. Nature herself, as we have said, teaches the choice of the proper measure.

Homer is admirable in every way, and he has a special merit: he is the only poet who rightly understands what part he should take himself. The poet should say as little as possible in his own person, since that is not what makes him an imitator. Other poets keep appearing on the scene themselves and imitate little and seldom. Homer, after a few prefatory words, at once brings in a man, or a woman, or some other personage, none of them lacking characteristic qualities, each having a character of his own.

The wonderful is required in Tragedy. The irrational, on which the wonderful chiefly depends, has wider scope in Epic poetry because there we do not see the person acting. The pursuit of Hector would be ludicrous on the stage, with the Greeks standing still instead of joining in the pursuit and Achilles waving them back; in the Epic poem the absurdity goes unnoticed. The wonderful is pleasing, as we can infer from the fact that everyone adds something of his own when telling a story, knowing that his hearers like it. Homer above all taught other poets how to tell lies skillfully. The secret lies in a fallacy. Men assume that if one thing is or becomes, a second is or becomes; so they imagine that if the second is, the first also is or becomes. But that is a false inference. Hence, when the first thing is untrue, there is no need, provided the second is true, to add that the first is or has become; for the mind, knowing the second to be true, falsely infers that the first is true as well. The Bath Scene of the Odyssey has an example of this.

The poet should accordingly prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities. The tragic plot must not be made of irrational parts. Everything irrational should be excluded if possible; or at any rate it should lie outside the action of the play (as, in the Oedipus, the hero's ignorance of how Laius died), not inside the drama — as in the Electra, the messenger's account of the Pythian games, or, in the Mysians, the man who has come from Tegea to Mysia and is still speechless. To plead that the plot would otherwise have been ruined is ridiculous: such a plot should not be constructed in the first place. But once the irrational has been introduced and made to look likely, we must accept it despite its absurdity. Even the irrational incidents in the Odyssey, where Odysseus is put ashore on Ithaca, show this: an inferior poet handling the subject would make plain how intolerable they might have been. As it is, the poet's charm veils the absurdity.
Diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where neither character nor thought is expressed. Conversely, a diction that is too brilliant only obscures character and thought.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 — Critical objections answered
paragraphs: Critical difficulties and their solutions can be drawn from a certain number of sources, and their number and nature can be set out as follows.

The poet is an imitator, like a painter or any other artist, so he must always imitate one of three kinds of objects — things as they were or are, things as people say or think they are, or things as they ought to be. He expresses them in language, using either current terms or, it may be, rare words or metaphors. There are also many modifications of language, and we allow these to poets. Add to this that the standard of correctness is not the same in poetry as in politics, any more than it is the same in poetry as in any other art. Within the art of poetry itself there are two kinds of faults: those that touch its essence, and those that are accidental. Suppose a poet has chosen to imitate something, <but has imitated it incorrectly> through lack of capacity. Then the error is inherent in the poetry. But suppose the failure comes from a wrong choice — he has represented a horse as throwing out both its off legs at once, or has made technical inaccuracies in medicine, for example, or in some other art. Then the error is not essential to the poetry. These are the points of view from which we should consider and answer the objections the critics raise.

First, take the matters that concern the poet's own art. If he describes the impossible, he commits an error. But the error may be justified if it achieves the end of the art (the end being the one already mentioned), that is, if it makes the effect of this part of the poem, or of any other part, more striking. A case in point is the pursuit of Hector. If, however, the end could have been reached as well or better without breaking the special rules of the poetic art, the error is not justified. For every kind of error should be avoided, if possible.

Again, we should ask whether the error touches the essentials of the poetic art or only some accident of it. For example — not to know that a hind has no horns is a less serious matter than to paint it inartistically.

Further, suppose the objection is that the description is not true to fact. The poet may perhaps reply, 'But the objects are as they ought to be.' In the same way Sophocles said that he drew men as they ought to be, and Euripides drew them as they are. In this way the objection may be met. Suppose, however, that the representation is of neither kind. The poet may then answer, 'This is how men say the thing is.' This applies to tales about the gods. It may well be that these stories are neither higher than fact nor true to fact; very possibly they are what Xenophanes says of them. But in any case, 'this is what is said.' Again, a description may be no better than the fact: 'still, it was the fact.' An example is the passage about the arms: 'Upright upon their butt-ends stood the spears.' This was the custom then, as it still is among the Illyrians.

Again, we may be examining whether something said or done by someone is poetically right or not. We must not look only at the particular act or saying and ask whether it is poetically good or bad. We must also consider who says or does it, to whom, when, by what means, and for what end — for instance, whether it is to secure a greater good or to avert a greater evil.

Usage of language resolves other difficulties. Sometimes the key is a rare word, as in {omicron upsilon rho eta alpha sigma / mu epsilon nu / pi rho omega tau omicron nu}. Here the poet perhaps means by {omicron upsilon rho eta alpha sigma} not mules but sentinels. The same applies to Dolon: 'ill-favoured indeed he was to look upon.' The poet does not mean that Dolon's body was ill-shaped; he means that his face was ugly, since the Cretans call a fair face {epsilon upsilon epsilon iota delta epsilon sigma}, 'well-favoured.' Again, {zeta omega rho omicron tau epsilon rho omicron nu / delta epsilon / kappa epsilon rho alpha iota epsilon}, 'mix the drink livelier,' is not an order to 'mix it stronger,' as if for hard drinkers, but to 'mix it quicker.'

In other cases the expression is a metaphor. Take 'Now all gods and men were sleeping through the night.' The poet says in the same breath: 'Often indeed as he turned his gaze to the Trojan plain, he marvelled at the sound of flutes and pipes.' The word 'all' stands metaphorically for 'many,' because all is a species of many. In the same way, in the verse — 'alone she hath no part...,' {omicron iota eta}, 'alone,' is a metaphor, because we may call the best known the only one.

Sometimes the solution depends on accent or breathing. Hippias of Thasos, for example, solved the difficulties in the lines — {delta iota delta omicron mu epsilon nu (delta iota delta omicron mu epsilon nu) delta epsilon / omicron iota,} and { tau omicron / mu epsilon nu / omicron upsilon (omicron upsilon) kappa alpha tau alpha pi upsilon theta epsilon tau alpha iota / omicron mu beta rho omega} — in this way.
Sometimes punctuation settles the question, as in Empedocles — 'Of a sudden things became mortal that before had learnt to be immortal, and things unmixed before mixed.'

Sometimes the cause of the difficulty is an ambiguity of meaning — as in {pi alpha rho omega chi eta kappa epsilon nu / delta epsilon / pi lambda epsilon omega / nu upsilon xi}, where the word {pi lambda epsilon omega} can be taken in two ways.

Sometimes the usage of language is the answer. People call any mixed drink {omicron iota nu omicron sigma}, 'wine,' and so Ganymede is said 'to pour the wine to Zeus,' although the gods do not drink wine. People likewise call workers in iron {chi alpha lambda kappa epsilon alpha sigma}, which means workers in bronze. This, however, could also be taken as a metaphor.

Again, a word may seem to contain some inconsistency of meaning. We should then ask how many senses it can have in that particular passage. Take 'there was stayed the spear of bronze': we should ask in how many ways we can understand 'being checked there.' The right method of interpreting is exactly the opposite of the one Glaucon describes. Critics, he says, jump to groundless conclusions. They first pass an adverse judgment, and then reason from it. They assume that the poet has said whatever they themselves happen to think, and they find fault when something conflicts with their own fancy. The question about Icarius has been handled in this way. The critics imagine that he was a Lacedaemonian, and so they think it strange that Telemachus did not meet him when he went to Lacedaemon. But the Cephallenian story may perhaps be the true one. The Cephallenians claim that Odysseus married a wife from among them, and that her father was Icadius, not Icarius. So the objection owes its plausibility merely to a mistake.

In general, three things can justify the impossible: the requirements of art, the higher reality, and received opinion. As for the requirements of art, a probable impossibility is preferable to an improbable possibility. Again, men such as Zeuxis painted may be impossible. 'Yes,' we reply, 'but the impossible is the higher thing, because the ideal type must surpass the reality.' The irrational we justify by appealing to what people commonly say. We also argue that the irrational sometimes does not violate reason, just as 'it is probable that a thing may happen contrary to probability.'

When things sound contradictory, we should test them by the same rules as in dialectical refutation: is the same thing meant, in the same relation, and in the same sense? We should therefore settle the question by what the poet himself says, or by what an intelligent person tacitly assumes.

Critics rightly censure the irrational, and likewise depravity of character, when there is no inner necessity for bringing them in. Examples are the irrational element in Euripides' introduction of Aegeus, and the badness of Menelaus in the Orestes.

Thus critical objections come from five sources. Critics censure things as impossible, or irrational, or morally hurtful, or contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness. The answers should be looked for under the twelve heads mentioned above.

chapters.title: Chapter 26 — Epic vs tragedy: which is higher?
paragraphs: Someone may ask which mode of imitation is the higher, the Epic or the Tragic. Suppose the more refined art is the higher, and the more refined art is always the one that appeals to the better sort of audience. Then the art that imitates anything and everything is clearly the most unrefined. On this view, audiences are too dull to follow unless the performers add something of their own, and so the performers move about restlessly. Bad flute-players twist and twirl when they must represent 'the quoit-throw,' and they jostle the coryphaeus when they play the 'Scylla.' Tragedy, people say, has this same defect. Compare what the older actors thought of their successors. Mynniscus used to call Callippides an 'ape' for the extravagance of his action, and people held the same opinion of Pindarus. Tragic art as a whole, they conclude, stands to Epic as the younger actors stand to the elder. Epic poetry, we are told, addresses a cultivated audience that has no need of gesture, while Tragedy addresses an inferior public. Since Tragedy is unrefined, it is evidently the lower of the two.

Now, to begin with, this accusation is aimed not at the poet's art but at the actor's. A reciter of epic can overdo gesture just as much, as Sosistratus did, and so can a singer in a lyrical competition, as Mnasitheus the Opuntian did. Next, we should not condemn all action, any more than all dancing, but only the action of bad performers. That was the fault found in Callippides, and it is found in others of our own day, who are censured for representing degraded women. Again, Tragedy, like Epic poetry, produces its effect even without action; reading alone shows its power. So if Tragedy is superior in all other respects, we say that this fault does not belong to it.

It is superior, and the reasons are these. It has all the epic elements — it may even use the epic meter. It also has music and spectacular effects as important accessories, and these produce the most vivid of pleasures. Further, it is vivid in reading as well as in representation. Moreover, it attains the end of the art within narrower limits, and a concentrated effect is more pleasurable than one that is spread over a long time and so diluted. Consider, for example, what would become of the Oedipus of Sophocles if it were cast in a form as long as the Iliad. Once more, the Epic imitation has less unity, and this is shown by the fact that any Epic poem supplies subjects for several tragedies. So when the poet adopts a story of strict unity, he must either tell it briefly and make it seem truncated, or, if he follows the Epic canon of length, make it seem weak and watery. <Such length implies some loss of unity,> by which I mean that the poem is built out of several actions, as the Iliad and the Odyssey are, with many such parts, each having a certain magnitude of its own. Yet these poems are as perfectly constructed as possible, and each is, as far as can be attained, an imitation of a single action.

Tragedy, then, is superior to Epic poetry in all these respects. It also fulfils its specific function better as an art, for each art ought to produce not any chance pleasure but the pleasure proper to it, as already stated. It plainly follows that Tragedy is the higher art, because it attains its end more perfectly.

That may suffice on Tragic and Epic poetry in general: their several kinds and parts, the number of each and their differences; what makes a poem good or bad; and the critics' objections with the answers to them.
